goals: Use DBSCAN to label noise and outliers
why: DBSCAN finds clusters of any shape and marks outliers automatically: GPS hotspots, fraud rings, sensor anomalies. No need to choose k.
explain: A point is a **core point** if at least **min_samples** points lie within radius **eps** of it. Core points that are close to each other join the same cluster, so clusters grow through dense regions.
Points near a cluster but not dense themselves are **border** points. Everything else is **noise** (label −1).
Like crowds at a festival: dense groups form clusters, scattered wanderers are noise.
Tuning: set min_samples ≈ 2 × the number of features; pick eps from the "knee" of a k-distance plot. It struggles when clusters have very different densities (try HDBSCAN).

example.title: Delivery hotspots from GPS points
steps: Dense areas such as markets and tech parks → clusters of any shape, even along roads
Result: 7 hotspots, 4% of points labelled noise
example.result: K-means would have forced every point into a round cluster, including the outliers.

mistakes: A single eps for clusters of very different density.
Treating noise points as errors when they may be the interesting anomalies.
takeaways: No k needed; finds any shape
use: Arbitrary shapes, outlier detection, spatial data

practice.code:
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, KMeans
X, _ = make_moons(400, noise=0.06, random_state=0)
print("DBSCAN labels:", set(DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=8).fit(X).labels_))
print("k-means splits the moons badly:", KMeans(2, n_init=10, random_state=0).fit(X).labels_[:10])

check.q: Which shape suits DBSCAN better than k-means?
